KEY MESSAGE 1...
Latest GOES Water Vapor imagery continues to reflect the slow
approach of an upper-level low from western New York. Meanwhile,
the latest SPC Mesoscale Analysis places a strengthening surface
cyclone just off the coast of Cape Cod, extending an inverted
trough westward across the northern portion of our CWA. Aloft,
strong divergent flow enhances the necessary forcing to sustain
scattered rain showers currently seen throughout eastern New
York and western New England. Enhanced low-level convergence
associated with the inverted surface trough, along with an
appreciable band of FGEN along the baroclinic zone at 850 mb, 
has organized a fair portion of these showers into a band that 
is currently pivoting through portions of the Eastern Catskills,
Mohawk Valley, and Southern Adirondacks. In these areas, 
roughly 0.1" to 0.3" of rain has fallen over the last three 
hours. 

With the upper-level low continuing to slowly track eastward
amid the aforementioned surface low pushing north-northeastward,
this band of rain is anticipated, and is already beginning, to 
pivot such that its southern extent will swing northeastward
into the Upper-Hudson Valley. In doing so, higher rainfall
totals are expected to fall over portions of Herkimer County,
adjacent to the pivot point to our west, initially. As the band
continues to pivot, a more persistent axis of rain will develop throughout
portions of the Mohawk Valley and Upper-Hudson Valley where
rainfall totals were increased slightly, in addition to Herkimer
County, with this update. Still, storm total rainfall amounts of
~0.3" to 0.7" in these areas will not pose any threats of
flooding given our recent, very dry stretch of weather.
Elsewhere, rainfall totals will reach less than 0.1" to about
0.3" except within Southern Vermont where 0.25" to 0.5" will be
possible due to orographic enhancement. 

As this system is rather slow moving, showers associated from
both the band and persistent moist, cyclonic flow will continue
through the remainder of the afternoon, through this evening,
and into the overnight period. By daybreak tomorrow, however,
the upper-level low will have departed into New England,
yielding height rises in the face of a building shortwave ridge.
Dry conditions will therefore return to the region and remain in
place through the day. Sufficient mixing courtesy of increasing
subsidence induced by the ridge will allow high temperatures to
reach the mid/upper 40s to low 50s across higher elevations with
mid 50s to pockets of 60 in the valleys. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...
Multiple shortwaves are anticipated to track through the region
beginning tomorrow night through Wednesday, leading to the
potential for additional rounds of scattered, light, and non-
impactful showers. That said, the most potent disturbances will
rotate through tomorrow night and Monday, leading to the next best
chances for precipitation. Most of the showers look to be
confined to lake-adjacent and higher terrain areas as west to
west-northwesterly flow will induce a lake response amid cold
air advection. And while most of these showers will again
predominantly be rain, a few snowflakes could mix into the
Adirondacks tomorrow night and Monday. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...
Medium- to long-range deterministic and ensemble guidance
continues to align in the portrayal of a large-scale trough
developing towards the end of the upcoming week. According to
the latest NAEFs, by Thursday, upper-level; mid-level; and low-
level heights look to fall to roughly 1-2 STDEVs below normal.
The direct impact of this outcome will be temperatures dipping
below normal Thursday and Friday, though only by about 0.5 to 1
STDEV as of this update. 

Precipitation chances during this time are highly uncertain.
Consequently, precipitation types are also highly uncertain.
While there is a storm system being resolved in the guidance as
potentially impacting the region, possibly as early as Thursday,
there is little agreement not only between the various models, 
but their individual run-to-run solutions in its evolution. The
evolution and resulting outcome of this storm is going to be 
highly dependent on the strength, orientation, and timing of the
aforementioned developing trough. The uncertainty that these
details retain at this great a lead time justify the very low
confidence in that storm system. However, we will continue to
monitor trends closely over the coming week.
